```{r}

#| include: false

# columns wide, so that with knitr's "#> " it fits pkgdown's code box.
options(
  width = 76,
  cli.num_colors = 1,
  cli.dynamic = FALSE,
  cli.progress_show_after = Inf

```

`inla_vanilla()` works on an unconstrained scale: a standard deviation goes
in as its log, a probability as its logit, a correlation as its inverse
hyperbolic tangent. Those are the right scales to compute on, and the wrong
ones to read. A posterior mean of $-0.42$ for $\log\sigma$ takes a moment to
turn into a statement about $\sigma$.

So name a parameter for the scale it is on, and the results come back on its
natural scale:

| Name in `init` | `logpost` receives | Reported as | For |
|---|---|---|---|
| `log_sigma` | $\vartheta = \log\sigma$ | `sigma` $= e^{\vartheta}$ | a positive parameter: an SD, a variance, a precision, a rate, a shape |
| `logit_p` | $\vartheta = \log\{p / (1 - p)\}$ | `p` $= 1 / (1 + e^{-\vartheta})$ | a parameter between 0 and 1: a probability, a proportion |
| `atanh_rho` | $\vartheta = \operatorname{artanh}\rho$ | `rho` $= \tanh\vartheta$ | a parameter between $-1$ and 1: a correlation |

The rule is short. You write on the unconstrained scale: `logpost`, `grad`,
`hess`, the `loglik` of `loo()` and the `fun` of `sampling()` all receive the
parameter under the name you gave it. You read on the natural scale:
`print()`, `summary()`, `coef()`, `plot()` and the draws of `sampling()` all
show the parameter without its prefix.

## A rate

Seven Poisson counts, with a $\mathrm{Gamma}(2, 1)$ prior on their rate
$\lambda$. The posterior is $\mathrm{Gamma}(2 + \sum_i y_i, 1 + n)$, so there
is an exact answer to compare with. The log-posterior is written on
$\vartheta = \log\lambda$, and the parameter is called `log_rate`:

```{r}
#| label: rate
library(inlavanilla)

y <- c(2, 0, 3, 1, 4, 2, 1)
logpost <- function(theta, y) {
  rate <- exp(theta[["log_rate"]])
  sum(dpois(y, rate, log = TRUE)) +
    dgamma(rate, 2, 1, log = TRUE) + # prior on the rate ...
    theta[["log_rate"]] # ... and its Jacobian
}
fit <- inla_vanilla(logpost, init = c(log_rate = 0), y = y, silent = TRUE)
fit
```

The row is `rate`, not `log_rate`, and the line under the table says how it
was obtained. Against the exact gamma posterior:

```{r}
#| label: rate-exact
shape <- 2 + sum(y)
rate <- 1 + length(y)
rbind(
  inlavanilla = fit$summary["rate", ],
  exact = c(
    shape / rate,
    sqrt(shape) / rate,
    qgamma(c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975), shape, rate),
    (shape - 1) / rate
  )
)
```

`plot()` draws the marginal on the natural scale too. The dashed curve is the
Laplace approximation carried to the same scale: a Gaussian for the log rate
is a log-normal for the rate.

```{r}
#| label: rate-plot
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-alt: "The posterior density of the rate, skewed to the right, with the Laplace log-normal density close to it, its right tail a little heavier."
plot(fit)
```

## What is mapped back, and how

Nothing in the fit changes. The mode, the covariance, the VB correction, the
skew-normal scans and the log marginal likelihood are all computed on the
scale of `logpost`, exactly as they would be under any other name. Each
natural-scale row is then worked out from that parameter's fitted skew-normal
alone.

The quantiles are the fitted quantiles passed through the transform, since
all three transforms are increasing. The mean, the SD and the mode are not:
they are those of the distribution of the natural-scale parameter. `summary()`
takes `transform = FALSE` to show the fit as `logpost` sees it, which makes
the difference plain:

```{r}
#| label: both-scales
on_log <- summary(fit, transform = FALSE)$table
on_log
cols <- c("Mean", "2.5%", "50%", "97.5%", "Mode")
rbind(
  rate = fit$summary["rate", cols],
  `exp(log_rate)` = exp(on_log["log_rate", cols])
)
```

The quantiles agree. The mean of the rate is above the exponential of the
mean of its log, and its mode is below the exponential of the mode, as the
exact gamma posterior confirmed above.[^moments]

[^moments]: For the log, the mean and SD come in closed form, from the moment
    generating function of the skew-normal. For the other two they are a
    one-dimensional integral, taken numerically. The mode is found by
    maximising the density of the natural-scale parameter. None of this calls
    `logpost`.

The diagnostics are different. They judge the approximation, which is made
on the scale of `logpost`, so they stay there and keep the names of `init`:

```{r}
#| label: diagnostics
diagnostics(fit, type = "param")[, c("names", "nmad", "alpha")]
```

`plot(fit, type = "sn_fit")`, which shows each skew-normal fit against its
scan, is on that scale as well.

### The Jacobian is still yours

The name changes how results are reported. It does not change what `logpost`
means. `logpost` is still the log density of the parameter it receives, so a
prior stated for the rate still needs its log-Jacobian, the
`+ theta[["log_rate"]]` above. Leaving it out targets a different posterior,
and nothing downstream can tell.

## Several parameters

The sepal lengths and widths of the 50 *setosa* irises, as a bivariate
normal. There are two means, two standard deviations and a correlation. The
standard deviations get $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ priors and the correlation a
uniform one, each with its Jacobian:

```{r}
#| label: bvn
setosa <- iris[iris$Species == "setosa", ]
x <- as.matrix(setosa[, c("Sepal.Length", "Sepal.Width")])

logpost_bvn <- function(theta, x) {
  mu <- theta[c("mu1", "mu2")]
  sigma <- exp(theta[c("log_sigma1", "log_sigma2")])
  rho <- tanh(theta[["atanh_rho"]])
  z1 <- (x[, 1] - mu[1]) / sigma[1]
  z2 <- (x[, 2] - mu[2]) / sigma[2]
  loglik <- -nrow(x) * (log(2 * pi) + sum(log(sigma)) + log1p(-rho^2) / 2) -
    sum(z1^2 - 2 * rho * z1 * z2 + z2^2) / (2 * (1 - rho^2))
  logprior <- sum(dnorm(mu, 0, 10, log = TRUE)) +
    sum(dexp(sigma, 1, log = TRUE)) +
    sum(log(sigma)) + # Jacobian of each SD
    log(0.5) + # uniform prior on rho ...
    log1p(-rho^2) # ... and its Jacobian
  loglik + logprior
}

init <- c(mu1 = 5, mu2 = 3, log_sigma1 = 0, log_sigma2 = 0, atanh_rho = 0)
fit_bvn <- inla_vanilla(logpost_bvn, init, x = x, silent = TRUE)
fit_bvn
```

The means are reported as they are, and the other three on their natural
scales. The interval for the correlation stays inside $(-1, 1)$, and is
longer on the side away from 1: an interval that is nearly symmetric on
Fisher's $z$ is squeezed towards 1 when it is carried back.

```{r}
#| label: bvn-plot
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-alt: "Five posterior densities: two symmetric ones for the means, two slightly right-skewed ones for the standard deviations, and a left-skewed one for the correlation."
plot(fit_bvn)
```

`fit$transform` records what was read from the names:

```{r}
#| label: transform-table
fit_bvn$transform
```

### Draws and derived quantities

`sampling()` returns draws on the natural scale, under the natural names:

```{r}
#| label: draws
set.seed(1)
draws <- sampling(fit_bvn, nsamp = 10000)
head(draws, 3)
```

A quantity of one parameter can be taken straight from them. A quantity of
several is what `fun` is for. `fun` is written like `logpost`: it receives
each draw on the unconstrained scale, under the names of `init`. Here is the
covariance of the two measurements, and the slope of the regression of width
on length:

```{r}
#| label: derived
derived <- sampling(fit_bvn, nsamp = 10000, fun = function(theta) {
  sigma <- exp(theta[c("log_sigma1", "log_sigma2")])
  rho <- tanh(theta[["atanh_rho"]])
  c(
    covariance = rho * sigma[[1]] * sigma[[2]],
    slope = rho * sigma[[2]] / sigma[[1]]
  )
})
t(apply(derived, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)))
```

The sample covariance is `r round(cov(x)[1, 2], 3)` and the least-squares
slope `r round(cov(x)[1, 2] / var(x[, 1]), 3)`, both well inside their
intervals.

This is also the answer for anything that is not a one-to-one map of a single
parameter. A covariance matrix, for one, ties its entries together, and no
entry can be mapped back on its own. The [correlation matrices
article](correlation.html) builds one from unconstrained parameters and reads
it back through the draws.

## Which scale to use

The three transforms are the usual choices, and they are the ones R-INLA
makes for its own hyperparameters (Rue et al., 2009). Of the 291
hyperparameters that R-INLA (version 26.11) keeps on a transformed scale, 265
are on one of these: the log for 179 (precisions, shapes, ranges), the logit
for 41 (probabilities), and for 45 correlations
$\log\{(1 + \rho) / (1 - \rho)\}$, which is twice Fisher's $z$. They are
good scales for this method for the reason they are good for INLA: on them a
posterior is usually close to Gaussian, and each skew-normal has only the
remaining skewness to pick up.

A few points on choosing:

* **A standard deviation, a variance or a precision.** Their logs differ only
  by a constant factor ($\log\sigma^2 = 2\log\sigma$,
  $\log\tau = -2\log\sigma$), and a skew-normal rescaled is still a
  skew-normal, so the three give the same approximation. Use the one your
  prior and likelihood are written in, and name it accordingly: `log_sigma`
  is reported as the SD, `log_var` as the variance.
* **The name is taken literally.** The part after the prefix is the name of
  what is reported, and it is the exponential, the inverse logit or the
  hyperbolic tangent of the parameter, whatever that is. A degrees-of-freedom
  parameter $\nu > 2$ written as $\vartheta = \log(\nu - 2)$ and named
  `log_nu` would be reported as $\nu - 2$ under the name `nu`. Call it
  `log_nu_minus_2`, or give it a name with no prefix and take $\nu$ from the
  draws.
* **Other bounds.** A parameter on an interval $(a, b)$, or with a lower
  bound other than zero, has no prefix. Write the transform into `logpost`,
  with its Jacobian, and use `sampling(fit, fun = ...)` for the natural
  scale.
* **No transform at all.** Means, regression coefficients and anything else
  that can take any real value need no prefix and are reported as they are.

## The rules for names

A prefix counts when it is `log_`, `logit_` or `atanh_`, in lower case,
followed by at least one more character. So `log_sigma`, `log_sigma[2]` and
`logit_p_treated` are transformed, and `logistic`, `log_`, `Log_sigma`,
`logsigma` and `my_log_sigma` are not.

A name that would clash is left alone. With parameters `log_sigma` and
`sigma` in the same model, both rows would be called `sigma`, so `log_sigma`
stays on the log scale and the fit warns once, naming it.

To switch the whole thing off, fit with `transform = FALSE`. Every parameter
is then reported as `logpost` receives it:

```{r}
#| label: switch-off
fit_off <- inla_vanilla(
  logpost,
  init = c(log_rate = 0),
  y = y,
  transform = FALSE,
  silent = TRUE
)
fit_off
```

The two fits are the same fit. `summary()`, `plot()` and `sampling()` take
`transform = FALSE` as well, so there is no need to refit to see the other
scale:

```{r}
#| label: switch-off-methods
set.seed(1)
head(sampling(fit_bvn, nsamp = 3, transform = FALSE))
```

Only these three transforms are recognised for now, and a model cannot yet
add its own.
